title: Model Serving Patterns
summary: Getting a trained model into production — the serving patterns and safe-rollout mechanics behind every production ML system.

slides.subTitle: Genuinely different infrastructure
slides.markdown: **Batch inference** runs predictions on a large set of inputs on a schedule (nightly, hourly) and stores the results for later use — no request waits for the model in real time. **Online (real-time) inference** serves predictions on demand, one request at a time, with a latency budget the caller is actively waiting on. This isn't just a config difference — it changes the infrastructure entirely: batch jobs optimize for throughput (process millions of rows cheaply, latency of any single row doesn't matter), while online serving optimizes for **tail latency** (the 99th-percentile response time under load matters more than average cost per prediction). Picking the wrong one for your use case is a common early mistake: a recommendation feed that could be precomputed nightly doesn't need an expensive always-on real-time endpoint.

slides.subTitle: The basic online-serving pattern
slides.markdown: The standard way to expose a model for online inference: wrap it in a server process that accepts requests (REST/JSON is simplest and most universal; gRPC is faster and more efficient for high-throughput or internal service-to-service calls) and returns predictions. The server loads the model once at startup and keeps it in memory, so each request only pays the cost of the forward pass, not model-loading time. Frameworks like TensorFlow Serving, TorchServe, or a custom Flask/FastAPI wrapper all implement this same basic pattern — the model becomes just another microservice other parts of the system call over the network.

slides.subTitle: Reproducible deployment
slides.markdown: Packaging a model server into a **container** (Docker) bundles the model weights, the serving code, and every dependency version (framework, Python version, system libraries) into one deployable artifact. This solves the classic "it worked on my machine" problem: without containerization, a model that depends on a specific library version can silently break in production if the deployment environment differs even slightly from where it was developed and tested. Containers also make horizontal scaling straightforward — spin up more identical containers behind a load balancer to handle more traffic, with every replica guaranteed to behave identically.

slides.subTitle: De-risking a new model version
slides.markdown: **Shadow deployment**: the new model runs alongside the current production model on real traffic, but its predictions are logged only, never returned to users — this lets you compare the new model's behavior against the old one at zero user-facing risk before it ever affects a real decision. **Canary release**: the new model is given a small slice of real traffic (say 5%) whose predictions *are* used, while the rest still goes to the old model; if monitoring shows the canary performing well, traffic is gradually ramped up, and if not, it's rolled back instantly. Shadow deployment answers "does the new model behave reasonably?" with zero risk; canary release answers "does it actually perform well for real users?" with limited, contained risk.

slides.sectionTitle: A/B testing a new model version
slides.subTitle: Safely comparing two models on real users
slides.markdown: A/B testing splits real traffic between the current model (control) and the new model (treatment), typically 50/50, over a period long enough to reach statistical significance on the metric that actually matters (conversion, revenue, click-through), not just an offline proxy metric like accuracy. Unlike a canary release (which is a risk-mitigation *rollout* mechanism, ramped based on operational health), A/B testing is a **measurement** exercise — its goal is a confident answer to "is the new model actually better?", including on business metrics an offline evaluation set can't capture, like whether higher predicted engagement actually translates to more revenue.

slides.subTitle: Matching the pattern to the product need
slides.markdown:
| | Online serving | Batch scoring |
|---|---|---|
| Latency requirement | Milliseconds, per request | None — hours are fine |
| Infrastructure | Always-on server, load balancer, scaling | Scheduled job, spins up and down |
| Cost profile | Pay for standby capacity even when idle | Pay only for compute during the run |
| Fits | Fraud scoring, live search ranking, chat | Nightly recommendation refresh, batch churn scoring |

How to decide: ask whether a prediction is needed the instant a request happens (fraud, live ranking) or can tolerate being precomputed on a schedule (weekly churn risk scores). Defaulting to online serving "just in case" adds real infrastructure cost and complexity for use cases that never actually needed the latency.

slides.sectionTitle: Real numbers: cold starts and the case for keeping servers warm
slides.markdown:
Loading a mid-size model (a few hundred MB to a few GB of weights) from disk into memory and initializing the runtime commonly takes 2-15 seconds — an eternity against a 100-200ms request latency budget. An autoscaler that scales a serving pod to zero when idle and spins one up fresh on the next request turns that occasional request into a multi-second timeout for whoever happens to trigger the cold start.

This is why online model servers are usually kept warm (a minimum replica count, never scaled to zero) even at idle cost, while batch scoring jobs — which don't have a live request waiting — can freely spin up and down, since a slow cold start just adds a few seconds to a job that already runs for minutes.

slides.sectionTitle: Serving many models on shared infrastructure
slides.subTitle: Multi-model servers
slides.markdown:
Running a dedicated always-on server per model works fine for a handful of models, but a platform with hundreds of models (one per customer, one per product category) makes that wasteful — most of those models get occasional traffic, not enough to justify a standing GPU each. A **multi-model server** loads several models into one serving process, swapping which model is active in memory based on which one is currently getting requests, sharing the underlying compute across many low-traffic models instead of dedicating hardware to each.

The trade-off is the same cold-start cost as before, now paid per model-swap rather than per deployment — multi-model serving trades guaranteed low latency for much better hardware utilization, which is the right trade only when most models are genuinely low-traffic.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: a canary that never had enough traffic to say anything
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "The canary got 5% of traffic for a day and its error rate looked fine, so it's safe to ramp up."

**Why it's wrong:** 5% of traffic for a day can be a genuinely tiny absolute sample — for a feature with 10,000 daily requests, that's 500 canary requests, which may not be enough to detect a regression that only shows up on a rare input pattern (a specific customer segment, an edge-case input format) hit by a handful of requests a day.

**Correct model:** size the canary's traffic share and duration against how rare the failure you're trying to catch is, not just "felt long enough" — a clean-looking canary on too small a sample is absence of evidence, not evidence of absence.
